title: Posner–Schlossman Syndrome (PSS): The Glaucomatocyclitic Crisis
summary: A textbook-grade overview of PSS, a rare inflammatory hypertensive condition characterized by unilateral, recurrent bouts of markedly elevated IOP and mild anterior uveitis. Essential for differentiating from acute angle-closure and managing CMV-related trabeculitis.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Posner-Schlossman Syndrome (PSS), or Glaucomatocyclitic Crisis, is a clinical entity characterized by recurrent, unilateral episodes of mild non-granulomatous anterior chamber inflammation associated with disproportionately high intraocular pressure (often 40-60 mmHg). Between attacks, the IOP and the eye typically return to normal, though chronic damage can occur with frequent recurrences.

branches: Viral Trigger: CMV (most common DNA found in aqueous), HSV, VZV
Trabeculitis: Acute inflammation of the trabecular meshwork reducing outflow
Prostaglandin Release: High levels of PGE2 in aqueous during crises
Allergic/Vascular: History of migraine or vasomotor instability
Autoimmune: Association with HLA-Bw54 and HLA-Cw1

sections.title: Clinical Features: Symptoms
content: Mild ocular discomfort or 'fullness'
Blurred vision (due to corneal edema/Sattler's veil)
Colored halos around lights
Surprisingly white eye (despite high IOP)
Minimal photophobia compared to other uveitides
Self-limiting nature (hours to weeks)

rows: Acute elevation (40–60 mmHg); significantly higher than expected for AC reaction
Fine, white, 'stellate' KPs on the inferior endothelium; localized edema
Mild cells (1-2+), minimal flare; No synechiae (PAS or PS)
Open on gonioscopy; No neovascularization or debris
May be slightly dilated or sluggish compared to contralateral eye
Rare heterochromia; mild iris atrophy in long-standing cases

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (Essential)
2. Gonioscopy (Mandatory to rule out angle closure)
3. Slit Lamp with dilated fundus exam (C:D ratio)
4. Aqueous humor PCR (Testing for CMV/HSV/VZV DNA)
5. Visual Fields (SITA-Standard 24-2) for chronic monitoring
6. OCT-RNFL to assess for glaucomatous damage

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol
content: 1. Topical Beta-Blockers (Timolol 0.5% BID)
2. Alpha-Agonists (Brimonidine 0.2% TID)
3. Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (Dorzolamide 2% TID)
4. Topical Steroids (Prednisolone Acetate 1% QID for inflammation)
5. Oral Acetazolamide (Diamox 250mg) for refractory high IOP
6. Cycloplegics (rarely needed unless photophobia is significant)

sections.title: CMV-Specific Therapy (Advanced)
content: Consider in recurrent/refractory cases with PCR+ results
Topical Ganciclovir 0.15% gel (5-6 times daily)
Oral Valganciclovir 900mg BID (loading) then 450-900mg QD
Long-term prophylaxis may be required to prevent recurrence
Monitor CBC and LFTs for systemic antiviral toxicity

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Concerns
content: Developing Posterior Synechiae (Suggests a different diagnosis)
Progressive Optic Nerve Cupping (Requires aggressive IOP control)
Ciliary Flush (Suggests more severe anterior uveitis or AACG)
Constricted Angles on Gonioscopy
Poor response to aqueous suppressants

content.explanation: P: Pressure is sky-high; S: Stellate KPs (minimal); S: Self-limiting & Solitary (unilateral).

sections.title: Surgical & Laser Considerations
content: Surgical intervention is rarely needed for acute crisis
Trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C: If optic nerve damage progresses despite meds
Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDD): Secondary option if trabeculectomy fails
Note: LPI (Laser Peripheral Iridotomy) is NOT indicated as the angle is open

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Chronic Secondary Open-Angle Glaucoma (25% of long-term cases)
Optic nerve atrophy/cupping from cumulative pressure spikes
Corneal endothelial cell loss over time
Prognosis is generally excellent if IOP is managed during spikes

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The IOP elevation in PSS is out of proportion to the mild AC reaction (1+ cell).
Avoid Pilocarpine: It can exacerbate inflammation and break the blood-aqueous barrier.
Prostaglandin Analogs (PGAs): Use with caution as they might theoretically worsen uveitis, though evidence in PSS is mixed.
Always check the fellow eye: While unilateral, patients may have asymmetric optic nerve susceptibility.
In between attacks, the KPs disappear completely, unlike Fuchs Uveitis Syndrome where they persist.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The CMV Connection
sections.content: Recent landmark studies using PCR analysis of aqueous humor have revolutionized our understanding of PSS. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is now identified as the primary etiologic agent in many PSS cases. This has shifted the treatment paradigm for chronic or recurrent PSS toward the use of topical and systemic anti-virals (Ganciclovir/Valganciclovir), which have been shown to reduce the frequency of attacks and the need for glaucoma surgery.
